POLICY:

Exercise and Understanding of Individual Rights and Negotiation of Choices

SCOPE OF POLICY:

This policy applies to all Shared Support staff members, independent contractors, volunteers, individuals supported, persons designated by the individual to act on their behalf and court- appointed legal guardians.

STATEMENT OF POLICY:

Shared Support, Inc. is committed to ensuring that all individuals have knowledge and understanding of their individual rights. Shared Support will continually offer the support and encouragement necessary for individuals to make choices and decisions regarding situations governing their own lives. Shared Support, Inc. fully supports individuals in exercising their rights, unless such exercise violates another person’s rights or significantly jeopardizes the safety of the individual. When situations arise between individuals or between individuals and staff members, Shared Support will assist the individuals impacted to negotiate choices and resolve differences.

IMPLEMENTATION OF POLICY:

EXERCISE AND UNDERSTANDING OF INDIVIDUAL RIGHTS Initially upon enrollment into services and annually thereafter, the individual, a person designated by the individual to assist with decision-making on behalf of the person and court- appointed legal guardians will be advised, in writing, of their individual rights. Individuals, the person designated by the individual to act on their behalf and court-appointed legal guardians will be given a copy of the individual rights and a copy will be maintained in the individual’s record. Shared Support will make any accommodations necessary, based upon the communication needs of the individual, to assure their understanding of their individual rights and to actively exercise those rights. Accommodations include but are not limited to augmentative or alternative communication, interpreters, communication boards or books, symbol systems, and sign language No person will be reprimanded, punished or retaliated against for exercising their individual rights and Shared Support will continually support and encourage the person to actively engage in exercising their rights.

A court’s written order that restricts an individual’s rights shall be followed. An individual who has a court-appointed legal guardian, or who has a court order restricting the individual’s rights, shall be involved in decision-making in accordance with the court order. All individuals have the right to privacy of their person and belongings, including the right to lock their bedroom door. This right is reviewed at the time of entry into services and annually thereafter. If an individual chooses to lock their bedroom door, staff members will only be permitted to gain entry to the room with the individual’s express permission (staff member will knock and ask for the door to be unlocked) or in the event of one or more of the following instances:

1. Evacuation of the home is mandatory due to fire, carbon monoxide or potential of either of the two; 2. Emergency personnel (fire/police/EMT) must gain access to the bedroom; 3. The individual is experiencing a medical or behavioral emergency that requires assistance; 4. The individual has a recurring or chronic medical or behavioral history and staff has a reasonable suspicion to believe that the individual requires assistance. Shared Support, Inc. direct care staff members and independent contractors will be trained on participant rights initially upon hire/contract and annually thereafter, as well as the reporting of incidents including rights violations. No person will be deprived of their individual rights and all allegations involving alleged rights violations will be entered into the PA Department of Human Services EIM system and investigated within the timeframes mandated. NEGOTIATION OF CHOICES The ability to negotiate is a valuable and essential life skill. Negotiation involves both empathy and compromise and individuals who learn to negotiate acquire and learn the importance of these abilities. Staff members who teach and mentor negotiation skills to individuals are enhancing their confidence, self-esteem and social relationship skills. It is inevitable that as people reside together, work together or socialize with one another, choices will need to be made and varying opinions, and conflicts, will ensue. Shared Support, Inc. will assist individuals in negotiating choices when the choice will violate another person’s rights. In doing so, Shared Support, Inc. staff members will provide the level of services necessary to enable the individual to meet their outcomes as outlined in the Support Plan. Services include assuring that assistance, support and guidance (prompting, instruction, modeling and reinforcement) will be provided to enable the individual to develop and maintain positive relationships with other individuals, staff and community members. Negotiating choice and resolving differences may be stressful, but also present a teachable moment for those involved. Below are some strategies to help resolve conflict in the event an individual’s choice violates the rights of another person:

1. Find a common ground. Any discussion involving choice and negotiation of differences should start with establishing the common ground for each party involved. Find an intended goal that everyone can agree on. 2. Create a positive environment. Honest and respectful communication is key to resolving differences of opinion and negotiation of choice. Staff should model, in all communications, a high standard when negotiating in front of the individual for things such as purchases, repairs, etc. Conversations that begin with positive language like “I understand you are frustrated, and I am here to help you figure this out” will be most effective. 3. Fully involve the individual in the negotiation process. Ensure that you are asking what the individual thinks is an appropriate response to the problem and help the individual develop ways to move forward and be successful, while also learning a degree of flexibility. Assuring that the individual has maximum control and ownership over the problem and choice reinforces that her concerns are being heard and that you are present and ready to help. 4. Learn to look for opportunities to encourage others. Model kindness, respect and compassion, all of which foster more opportunities to negotiate and solve problems. IN CONCLUSION It is important for team members to remember that negotiation is a lifelong process and it is vital to take the time and make the effort to model and teach effective negotiation skills. It is also imperative to be mindful that individuals learn skills in differing ways. Shared Support, Inc. continues its commitment to person directed supports through the process of monthly Circle Meetings and that person specific strategies will be developed, as needed, through team collaboration at the meetings.

RE: Flushable Wipes

Just a reminder to please not flush wipes down the toilet, even if they say they

are “flushable’. They have caused multiple issues with clogging at our homes in

the past. Toilet paper is designed to disintegrate in the pipes and sewage

systems, but flushable wipes are not. (Companies can currently label wipes as

“flushable” simply because they aren’t restricted from doing so.) However, these

wipes are typically made with synthetic materials, plastics, or polyester, that won't

break down. So even if they flush down the toilet, they will eventually build up

and end up clogging the pipes. This can cause considerable costs to remove

these clogs. So, please make sure we are only flushing waste and toilet paper in

the toilets at the homes- wipes, sanitary items, and all other materials should be

disposed of in the trash.

Thank you!

POLICY:

Sexual Health, Personal Relationships and Sexuality

SCOPE OF POLICY:

This policy applies to all Shared Support, Inc. individuals, employees and independent contractors.

STATEMENT OF POLICY:

Shared Support, Inc. understands that people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (ID/DD) have sexual needs, feelings and identities and have the right to privacy and sexual expression. Sexuality includes not just sexual activity, but also the acknowledgement of feelings, displays of affection, ways of relating to self and others, self-esteem, gender identification and sexual orientation. Individuals with ID/DD have the need to love and to be loved and have the right to seek and develop consenting, intimate relationships with persons of their choice. We support people in expressing their sexuality so long as they are not injuring themselves or others and are capable of providing informed consent. Every individual has the right to be supported to develop safe and loving friendships and relationships, as well as to cohabitate with partners of choice and/or to marry. We understand that lack of awareness and information about sexuality leaves people with ID/DD vulnerable to sexual abuse. We are committed to ensuring that all individuals have the sufficient education and support to develop healthy sexuality and to protect them from abuse, exploitation, unwanted pregnancy and sexually transmitted disease.

IMPLEMENTATION OF POLICY:

INFORMATION AND EDUCATION Individuals Often people with ID/DD do not receive education on sexuality and acquire misinformation from friends and television. Many people do not wish to broach the subject of sexuality with individuals, denying individuals with ID/DD the opportunity to develop responsible social and sexual skills and behaviors, the right to exercise choice and the right to have their basic needs fulfilled. Lack of education surrounding human sexuality also leaves individuals naïve and vulnerable to sexual abuse or exploitation.

11/08/2018

When appropriate, the program team will provide ongoing education and information to an individual in a private setting, outside of team meeting settings, and at the level and pace that the person can best understand the information. Topics of education and information sharing may include, but is not limited to: informed decision making; safe sexual practices; sexual orientation; sexual abuse; how to tell the difference between friends, acquaintances and strangers; boyfriend/girlfriend issues as they arise; the difference between physical affection and sex; understanding body language; awareness of others; assertion and the ability to say “no” at any time; stopping sexual contact when a partner says “no”; laws related to sexual activity; changes and awareness of their own body; abstinence; sexual expression; recognizing and avoiding abuse; personal and sexual hygiene; preventing sexually transmitted disease; pregnancy and contraception; and marriage. Staff and Life Sharing Providers/Independent Contractors Staff and life sharers will receive initial and ongoing support and education surrounding the rights and needs of individuals with ID/DD to express their sexuality, develop loving and intimate relationships, and to freely express their gender identification and sexual orientation. Staff is instructed that, as situations surrounding sexuality arise for which they need direction, they are to seek the counsel of their direct supervisor. Staff and life sharers will allow individuals privacy in their bedrooms for intimate contact with partners, unless indicated otherwise in the person’s Individual Support Plan/Behavior Support Plan. People also have the right to privacy in their communications, including email, text and telephone calls, unless otherwise indicated in their Individual Support Plan/Behavior Support Plan. Staff and life sharers will respect that people have different sexual orientations and preferences and will accept that people with ID/DD may be heterosexual, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, monogamous or not monogamous with partners. Staff members will not interfere with sexual expression, as long as the sexual act is legal and involves consenting adults, and at no time are staff members and life sharers to impose their own personal value systems and beliefs upon individuals Shared Support, Inc. Supports the Pennsylvania Department of Human Services, Office of Development Programs Everyday Lives Values as They Apply to Sexual Health, Personal Relationships and Sexuality.

1. Individuals with disabilities are sexual human beings with their own cultural, religious/faith, ethnic and family values. 2. Individuals with disabilities have the right to enjoy their personal relationships and sexuality in a safe, consensual and legal manner, while respecting the rights of others. 3. Individuals with disabilities have the basic rights as individuals without disabilities to self-identify their gender, sexual orientation and sexual preferences. 4. Individuals with disabilities have the right to accessible and appropriate education, information and resources that address their individual personal relationships, sexual health and sexuality needs. 5. Individuals with disabilities have the right to privacy when accessing supports and have the right to have information about their personal relationships remain private unless they

11/08/2018

consent to a disclosure. Privacy covers all forms of communication. Information regarding an individual’s personal relationships, sexual health and sexuality should be considered private and must be treated with respect and dignity. 6. Individuals with disabilities have the right to enjoy relationships and to express their sexuality in a safe manner. 7. Individuals with disabilities have the right to have their sexual health and personal relationships supported by knowledgeable provider agency staff and a knowledgeable Individual Plan team.

RELATED POLICIES, PROCEDURES, FORMS, RESOURCES:

Pa DHS/ODP Bulletin 00-18-01. Guidelines Concerning Sexual Health, Personal Relationships, and Sexuality. Issue Date April 13, 2018.

11/26/2019 Ch. 6100.143. Annual Training

The Safe and Appropriate Use of Behavior Supports

Individuals living with a developmental disability are more vulnerable throughout their lives and experience alarmingly high rates of trauma. Because of their potentially limited knowledge, social skills and verbal skills, individuals are less likely to tell someone about a trauma and their capacity to heal is diminished. Many of the individuals supported by Shared Support, Inc. have experienced varying degrees of trauma throughout their lives, making it very difficult for them to trust other people and to build positive, long-term relationships. Shared Support expects the following characteristics to be consistently demonstrated by all staff while working with individuals:

  • Patience
  • Compassion
  • Kindness
  • Honesty
  • Respect
  • Forgiveness
  • Flexibility Understanding Negative Behavior. All negative behavior exhibited by an individual is non- verbal communication regarding an unmet need. A behavior is a means of getting to something, someone or someplace OR it is a way of getting away from something, someone or someplace (or both). It is the team’s role to work through negative behaviors, building trust with the individual, listening and documenting as necessary, in order to determine the unmet need and helping the person get the need met. Sometimes that process can occur quickly, while for other individuals it may take a great amount of time. As an individual’s need continues to be unmet, the person will increase the frequency, duration and intensity of the negative behavior(s) displayed until such as time as the need is met.

As negative behavior occurs, it is important to continually assess the individual to determine why he or she may be acting out. It is also important to assess the environment in which you are working to determine if anything surrounding the individual could be used to harm themself or another person (i.e. a baseball bat in the garage easily accessible to the person when in crisis).

Preventing a crisis situation is our primary focus. Listen and partner with the individual in order to encourage positive behaviors, promote the person to be active and engaged in activities of their choosing and continually assess and identify any stimulus triggers (things, noise, people, situations, etc. that may upset the person) so that you can remove or reduce that stimulus and eliminate a potential crisis.

De-escalation of a crisis situation may be necessary if you are unable to identify the stimulus trigger and a person begins acting out. Staff responsibility is to protect the individual to the best of their ability and to use the least amount of interaction necessary to secure the individual’s safety. Engage with the person calmly, actively listen to the person to identify the unmet need, offer reassurance and encouragement, ignore challenging questions posed by the individual and avoid overreacting to the individual’s behavior.

Recognize your own non-verbal communication by:

  • keeping an open and relaxed body posture (don’t cross your arms);
  • maintaining a safe distance from the person, allowing the individual their personal space;
  • balancing your height, if a person is shorter than you or in a wheelchair, by sitting down so that you are on their level;
  • keeping your facial expression relaxed, interested and non-judgmental;
  • maintaining eye contact to show that you are listening and alert;
  • allowing the person to speak and empathizing with them;
  • accepting and respecting the feelings that they are communicating;
  • allowing silence for reflection;
  • allowing adequate time for the person to make decisions;
  • not touching the person without first asking.

Recognize your verbal communication by:

  • being continually aware of the tone and volume of your voice, as well as your attitude;
  • using short sentences – do not be wordy when speaking with someone in crisis;
  • reflecting what the person is telling you by rephrasing and offering that thought back to the person to ensure you understand;
  • using People First language and always speaking with the individual in a respectful and courteous manner.

11/26/2019 Ch. 6100.143. Annual Training

Remember that a crisis is a crisis because the individual knows no response to deal with the situation they are facing.

Following a crisis event, debrief with the individual and other team members, such as fellow DSP staff, the Program Specialist and/or other members of the program team. Never blame or punish the individual or make the person feel inadequate because of their display of emotion. Remember, the role of the DSP is to listen, document findings and determine the unmet need in order to avert future crisis situations.

A person’s behavior only needs to be “changed” when it represents a danger to the person or to others or when the individual wants to change the behavior, as often a behavior may be an obstacle to the individual participating in community activities of their choice. It is not the role of the DSP or Shared Support to “control” individuals – our role it to support and encourage the individual to make healthy and safe choices that enable the individual to lead the life of their choosing.

Stress, anger and aggression must be understood in order to aptly support an individual and minimize crisis events. Anger and aggression, for instance, always stem from feelings including fear, embarrassment, shame, frustration, helplessness and/or loss. When under stress, our pulse and breathing quicken, while our ability to communicate effectively decreases, as do our listening and reasoning skills. As support staff, understanding these facts enables us to effectively partner with the individuals we support because, as we listen compassionately and build a trusting relationship with the individual, we lessen their feelings of hopelessness and distrust. The individuals we support must feel safe in order to lessen negative behaviors and enhance their overall quality of life.

Behavior Support Plan:

If a person has a formal behavior support plan, the best way you can interact with the person and promote their success is to adhere to the behavior support plan and offer feedback to the individual and their team on what is and what is not working for the individual. The behavior support plan is in place to assist the individual to identify their strengths and build upon those to meet their needs in the least structured manner possible.

Trauma

The longer we live, the more inevitable it is that we will experience trauma. Trauma is the response to a deeply distressing or disturbing event that overwhelms an individual’s ability to cope, causes feelings of helplessness, diminishes their sense of self and their ability to feel the full range of emotions and experiences. Trauma does not discriminate and is pervasive worldwide. There are no objective criteria to evaluate which events in a person’s life will cause post-trauma symptoms, but circumstances typically involve the loss of control, betrayal, abuse of power, helplessness, pain, confusion and /or loss.

Trauma for Individuals with Intellectual and Developmental Disorders

Over 70% of people with IDD report being victims of abuse

  • 90% of them said it occurred on multiple occasions
  • Only 37% reported the abuse to the authorities

People with IDD are 7 times more likely to be sexually abused than those without disabilities.

People with IDD are 2.5 times more likely to be victims of a violent crime and 40% more likely to have the perpetrators be someone they know.

(Reference – Center on Victimization & Safety)

Types of Trauma

Small “t” trauma - circumstances where one’s bodily safety or life is not threatened, but cause trauma nonetheless. Examples of this for people we support may include family violence, social exclusion, exclusion from the family, neighborhood violence, frequent changes in living arrangements / lack of stability.

Large “T” trauma – extraordinary experiences that bring about severe distress and helplessness. They may be one-time events, or they may be prolonged stressors. Examples of this for people we support may be sexual abuse, physical abuse, neglect, negative events, grief and loss. Large “T” traumas are more difficult or even impossible to overlook, yet they are often actively avoided. As an example, people may try to avoid triggers such as personal reminders, certain locations or situations. They also may resist confronting memories of the event.

Trauma and the Brain

When something happens in the present that reminds the person of the negative/traumatic past, the person’s brain automatically goes into a “fight or flight” mode, perceiving the person is in danger even when they are not in any danger whatsoever. This is a primitive response that the person is entirely unaware of.

1. Trauma -----------------------2. Sparks emotion -------------------3. Person exhibits behaviors When we only address the exhibited behavior, we miss the true root cause of the person’s difficulties.

Recognizing a Trauma Response vs a Behavior Response

Trauma Behavior

Triggered in an irrational manner Has a purpose and intent

Overreaction to a small event Deliberate – acting on environment to get a response Very emotion-based Intent is important in identifying the response Does not serve the person well Goal is to get something they want, can move them forward Does not move them forward You can typically identify the antecedent (trigger) Example: A person repeatedly reacts irrationally when visiting a particular family member. Example: A person reacts strongly when informed their plans to dine out have been cancelled due to bad weather/unsafe driving conditions. Common Responses and Symptoms of Trauma Although response to traumatic events vary significantly among individuals, below is a list of basic, common symptoms: Common emotional signs include:

  • Sadness
  • Anger
  • Denial
  • Fear
  • Shame These emotions may lead to:
  • Nightmares
  • Insomnia
  • Difficulty with relationships
  • Emotional outbursts Common physical symptoms include:
  • Nausea
  • Dizziness
  • Altered sleep patterns
  • Changes in appetite
  • Headaches
  • Gastrointestinal problems
  • Generalized pain disorders Common psychological disorders/symptoms include:
  • Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD)
  • Depression
  • Anxiety
  • Dissociative disorders
  • Substance abuse problems What People Need the Most – What You Can Do While there is no cure for trauma nor any quick fixes for the suffering and symptoms associated with it, there is hope and a wide range of effective trauma focused therapies, such as CBT (Cognitive Behavioral therapy), EMDR therapy (Eye Movement Desensitization therapy), Somatic Experiencing and Sensorimotor Psychotherapy. The individuals you support may also be prescribed medications such as antidepressants and anti-anxiety medications, both of which can make symptoms less intense and more manageable. Key ingredients that you as a direct care staff member can assist with include helping the individual to feel SAFE, EMPOWERED AND CONNECTED. Individuals who have experienced trauma need staff who can help provide them with a sense of safety in their homes, personal spaces and while in the community. Staff should exhibit understanding, kindness and empathy toward the individual, especially when they experience feelings of panic and their brain goes into that “fight or flight” mode described above, at which times individuals who have experienced trauma will most likely exhibit behaviors. A positive identify is important for all of us, including the people we support, and a continued focus upon what the person does well, what they are proud of, establishing friendships and assisting the individual to find avenues where they feel they make a difference (volunteering/employment) are all important steps in healing trauma. Staff members will be educated on the individual’s past, to the extent that Shared Support is aware, including any knowledge of past trauma and present-day signs and symptoms, as well as the support plan to address those signs and symptoms. In that the brain/body “stores” trauma, other avenues that the interdisciplinary team may explore to help an individual be present in their body may include yoga, acupuncture, dance, massage, etc.

What is Worker’s Compensation? Worker’s Compensation is a medical care and disability income benefit for those workers who are injured on-the-job. Your employer self-insures Workers’ Compensation via the Eagle Workers Compensation Trust. This means that instead of purchasing a Workers Compensation policy from an Insurer, your employer pays for lost wages & medical directly.

Is Worker’s Compensation the same as Health Insurance? No. Worker’s Compensation covers those injuries or illnesses which are related to your employment. Health insurance (such as Blue Cross; Aetna etc.) covers you when you are sick or injured outside the scope of employment.

What is covered by Worker’s Compensation? The Pennsylvania worker’s compensation benefits include but are not limited to the following:

1.

All necessary and reasonable medical expenses related to your injury, such as:

  • Doctor visits
  • X-rays
  • Physical Therapy*
  • Diagnostic Tests (MRI, CT, EMG)*
  • Prescriptions*
  • Surgery
  • Hospital stay *A network is established. Please refer to the Employer’s Panel Provider list.

2. Reimbursement for Lost Wages:

If you are medically unable to perform your employment duties, and panel physician has deemed you totally disabled, in most cases, you would receive 66 2/3% of difference in weekly wage before and after your injury subject to legal maximums.

Your employer may have a Return-to-Work program in which an effort is made to return you to your duties – or transitional duties –as soon as safely possible. History has shown that failure to do so results in an employee feeling less and less a part of the organization. This influences a person’s positive, healing attitude.

A job offer is made by your employer noting any specific restrictions. This is referred to Transitional Duty.

What happens now that I have reported the injury?

  • Visit a doctor from the list of qualified treating physicians that has been provided (your posted medical panel) during the first 90 days of treatment.
  • As necessary, cooperate in providing information to us, so that the claim can be processed as smoothly as possible.
  • Discuss with us, or your employer, any concerns that you may have about the process or the services which are being provided. We share with your employer the goal of assuring that your claim is handled as expediently and accurately as possible.
  • Our collective goal is to prevent workplace accidents. Your employer may perform investigation with the intent of determining the root causes of the accident. This will lead to the prevention of similar accidents. They may seek your assistance in this endeavor.

POLICY:

Incident Management

SCOPE OF POLICY:

This policy applies to all staff members, independent contractors and other Shared Support, Inc. stakeholders.

STATEMENT OF POLICY:

To provide a standard for procedures which serve to prevent, manage and report all incidents as defined by the Pennsylvania Office of Developmental Programs Bulletin #00-21-92 issued 03/01/2021, effective 07/01/2021. The primary goal of this policy is to ensure that responses to incidents ensure the health and safety of the individual/individuals involved using person centered practices. In addition, the continuous analysis and review of incidents will seek to enhance risk management processes and to formulate actions to prevent the recurrence of incidents.

IMPLEMENTATION OF POLICY:

I. Incident Reporting/Investigations

In addition to incidents being reported verbally, alleged and suspected incidents will also be reported. These include potential incidents suspected through observation of physical, behavioral or emotional indicators of abuse, neglect or another incident type. Additionally, trend analysis that reveals a pattern of injury, illness or other incidents that could be indicators of abuse, neglect or another incident type will be reported. Upon learning of an incident or alleged or suspected incident, Shared Support will take immediate action to protect the health, safety, rights and well-being of all individuals. Our actions may include dialing 911, removing or reducing an imminent risk to an individual and arranging for emergency or timely medical care. If an alleged target is identified and is associated with Shared Support as an employee, staff, volunteer, contractor, consultant or intern, the target will be separated from the individual, and all other individuals, pending the outcome of the investigation, as well as the completion of any corrective action steps specific to the target. If the alleged target is another individual receiving services and presents a reasonable expectation of ongoing risk to the victim, Shared Support will collaborate with the SCO and county ID/AE to identify strategies to protect the health, safety and ongoing rights of the victim.

A. The following are categories of incidents to be reported within 24 hours after the occurrence of the incident as

are indicated in the Pennsylvania Office of Developmental Programs Bulletin #00-21-02 for all waiver participants being supported by Shared Support, Inc at the time of incident occurrence.

1. ABUSE. A deliberate or careless act by a person, including another individual receiving services, which may result in mental or physical harm.

i. Misapplication/Unauthorized Use of Restraint (injury). The use of a restraint that does not follow ODP’s regulations, the misapplication of an approved restraint technique or the use of a restraint that results in an injury requiring treatment beyond first aid. Examples include:

Prone position restraint. Any restraint that inhibits digestion or respiration, inflicts pain, causes embarrassment or humiliation, causes hyperextension of joints, applies pressure on the chest or joints or allows for a free fall to the floor. Any physical restraint that is used more than 30 cumulative minutes within a two-hour period.

Chemical and mechanical restraints.

ii. Misapplication/Unauthorized Use of Restraint (no injury). The use of a restraint that does not follow ODPs regulatory requirements or the misapplication of an approved restraint technique. Examples of this are noted in i. above. iii. Physical abuse. An act which causes or may cause physical injury to an individual, such as striking or hitting. Physical injuries may or may not be present with physical abuse. Allegations of physical acts without obvious signs of injury must be reported. Monitoring or body checks may be necessary to look for signs of injury after initial discovery of the incident. In addition, injuries attributed to a staff person or another individual receiving services that require treatment beyond first aid or an inpatient admission to a hospital are to be reported as abuse.

If an incident involved an injury, common examples of situations that may be present with physical abuse include, but are not limited to:

A patterned bruise, no matter its size, that is in the shape of an identifiable object such as a belt buckle, shoe, hanger, fingermark, etc. Unexplained serious injuries or multiple bruises, cuts, abrasions. A spiral fracture. Dislocated joints. Bilateral bruising, which is bruising on both sides of the body (e.g., the top of both shoulders, both sides of the face or inside of both thighs). Bruising to an area of the body which does not typically or easily bruise (e.g., midline stomach, breasts, genitals, inner thighs or middle of the back). Injuries that are not consistent with what is reported to have happened. Injuries explained as caused by self-injury to parts of the body the individual has not previously injured or cannot access.

iv. Psychological abuse. An act which causes or may cause mental or emotional anguish by threat, intimidation, humiliation, isolation or other verbal or nonverbal conduct to diminish another. Examples include, but are not limited to:

Bullying, rejecting, degrading and terrorizing acts. Disregard for privacy during personal care. Paid caregiver ignoring an individual, including, but not limited to:

  • Active ignoring (that is not part of the approved plan) such as ignoring a call or

request for help/assistance.

  • Passive acts, such as non-essential use of a cellphone (or another electronic

device), watching TV, etc.

Threats of isolation. Yelling, name calling, blaming, shaming. Mimicking or mocking an individual’s voice, speech, behaviors, etc. Statements that are intended to humiliate or infantilize, including insults, threats of

abandonment or institutionalization and other controlling, dominant or jealous behavior. The act of taking, transmitting or displaying an electronic image (in any medium

including social media, personal computers, cell phones, etc.) of an individual that is intended to shame, degrade, humiliate or otherwise harm the personal dignity of the individual. When an individual witnesses an incident for which they were not the intended victim,

but it causes or has caused mental or emotional anguish.

v. Seclusion. The involuntary confinement of an individual in an area from which the individual is prevented from leaving. This includes verbal instruction or any explicit or implicit intimidation that indicates to an individual that he or she may not leave a room, regardless of whether the individual has the ability to physically remove himself or herself from the situation. Examples include, but are not limited to, the following prohibited acts:

Placing an individual in a locked room. A locked room includes a room with any type of engaged locking device such as a key lock, spring lock, bolt lock, foot pressure lock, device or object, or a person physically holding the door shut. Placing an individual in a room from which they are unable to exit independently due to the general accessibility of the room (i.e., wheelchair ramps, transitions, etc.), features of the door hardware (i.e., handles that do not meet the accessibility needs of the individual) or any other obstacle that prevents an individual from exiting.

2. BEHAVIORAL HEALTH CRISIS EVENT. An event or situation that exceeds the individual’s current resources and coping mechanisms that causes the individual to experience extreme disorganization of thought, hopelessness, sadness, confusion, panic or other emotional distress. The event includes actions(s) by an individual that pose a danger to themselves or others and are unable to be mitigated without the assistance of law enforcement, mental health or medical services.

Community-Based Crisis Response. An event in which law enforcement or emergency services respond to and resolve without transport to another location for intake, assessment or treatment. Facility-Based Crisis Response. An event in which law enforcement or emergency services respond to and an individual is transported to a psychiatric facility, including crisis facility, or the psychiatric department of an acute care hospital for evaluation or treatment that does not result in an admission. Immediate Arrest and Incarceration Crisis Response. An event in which law enforcement responds to a behavioral health crisis event and arrests, charges and incarcerates an individual without first obtaining a mental health evaluation/admission at a facility designated to provide such services. Psychiatric Hospitalization (involuntary). An involuntary inpatient admission to a psychiatric facility, including crisis facility, or the psychiatric department of an acute care hospital for evaluation or treatment. Psychiatric Hospitalization (voluntary). A voluntary inpatient admission to a psychiatric facility, including crisis facility, or the psychiatric department of an acute care hospital, for evaluation or treatment.

3. DEATH. All deaths are reportable. Deaths attributed to or suspected to have been the result of abuse or neglect require additional reporting in the appropriate corresponding category. In addition, any critical incidents that are discovered during an investigation into a death require additional reporting in the appropriate corresponding category.

Natural Causes – Services Provided. Primarily attributed to a terminal illness or an internal malfunction of the body not directly influenced by external forces. For example, a person who has been diagnosed with cancer, receives Hospice care or has a DNR order in place. A death should be reported in this category if it occurs while an individual is enrolled in a Waiver program or ACAP (Adult Community Autism Program) or is receiving services in a provider operated setting. Unexpected – Services Provided. An unexpected death is primarily attributed to an external unexpected force acting upon the individual. Deaths attributed to events such as car accidents, falls, homicide, choking and suicides would be considered unexpected. A death should be reported in this category if it occurs while an individual is enrolled in a Waiver program or ACAP or is receiving services in a provider operated setting. Natural Causes – Only Supports Provided. Primarily attributed to a terminal illness or an internal malfunction of the body not directly influenced by external forces. For example, a person who

has been diagnosed with cancer and is receiving hospice services or when a DRN order is in place. Unexpected – Only Supports Provided. An unexpected death is primarily attributed to an external unexpected force acting upon the individual. Deaths attributed to events such as car accidents, falls, homicide, choking and suicides would be considered unexpected.

4. EXPLOITATION. An act or course of conduct by a person against an individual or an individual’s resources without informed consent or with consent obtained through misrepresentation, coercion, or threats of force, which results in monetary, personal or other benefit, gain or profit for the target, or monetary or personal loss to the individual. Exploitation should be reported regardless of the actual or perceived value of the loss.

Failure to Obtain Informed Consent. An intentional act or course of conduct by a person which results in the misuse of an individual’s consent or failure to obtain consent. Examples include, but are not limited to, signing on behalf of or coercing/deceiving an individual into applying for credit cards, signing contracts and signing loan documents, will and other items that relate to the personal property, money or identity of an individual. Material Resources. The illegal or improper act or process of a person using the material resources or possessions of an individual for his or her own personal benefit or gain. This includes but is not limited to misusing or stealing an individual’s possessions, soliciting gifts and coercing an individual to spend his or her funds for things he or she may not want or need, things for use by others or for the benefit of the household. Medical Responsibilities/Resources. An act or course of conduct of a person that results in an individual paying for medical care or items that are normally covered by insurance or other means. This includes, but is not limited to:

  • Requiring an individual to pay for a medical appointment, procedure or equipment due to

failure of the ISP team to provide support or resources to find a medical provider that accepts the individual’s insurance or whose services are covered by other means.

  • Requiring an individual to pay for an appointment, procedure or equipment when there is

a failure on the part of the service provider to support an individual to attend or schedule medical appointments or to maintain medical equipment.

Missing/Theft of Medications. Missing medications without explanation or theft of medications. Misuse/Theft of Funds. The illegal or improper act or process of a person using the funds of an individual for his or her own personal benefit or gain. This includes misuse or mismanagement by a representative payee or other responsible party, theft of money, SNAP benefits or soliciting monetary gifts from an individual. Room and Board. Requiring an individual to pay for items that are covered as part of room and board charges, charging more than allowable rates for room and board or charging for a service or support that is included in a rate for which a provider is or will be reimbursed. This includes any situation in which the individual is required to pay for the same item/service twice. Examples of items that are covered as part of the room and board residency agreement include, but are not limited to:

  • Standard toiletries including shampoo, deodorant, soap, toothpaste, etc.
  • Utility costs, including trash removal, lawn care and snow removal. o Household furniture. o Basic linens including blankets, towels, washcloths, sheets and pillowcases. o Cleaning, laundry and other household supplies. o One telephone with local telephone service. o Internet service. o Food choices of the individual, with consideration of the food cost and nutrition, including the individual’s preference, culture, religion and beliefs, and an individual’s prescribed diet, if the prescribed diet is not covered by the individual’s health care plan or another funding source. Prescribed dietary items necessary for individuals basic health and

nutrition include but are not limited to 1) products used to thicken liquids/foods; 2) phenylketonuria (PKU) diet foods; 3) meal replacement shakes and snacks; 4) diabetic diet foods.

  • Laundry of towels, bedding and the individual’s clothing.
  • Lawn care, food preparation, maintenance and housekeeping, including staff wages and

benefits to perform these tasks.

  • Meals provided away from the residential service location that are arranged by a staff

person in lieu of meals provided in the residential service location.

  • Incontinence products, if the incontinence product is not covered by the individual’s

health care plan or another funding source.

  • Building and equipment repair, renovation and depreciation.
  • Rent, taxes and property insurance.
  • Unpaid Labor. The illegal or improper act or process of a person who is using an individual to

perform unpaid labor that would otherwise be compensated in a manner consistent with labor laws.

5. FIRE. A situation that requires fire personnel or other safety personnel to extinguish a fire, clear smoke from the premises, etc. While not required, it is strongly recommended by ODP that situations in which staff extinguishes small fires without the involvement of fire personnel be reported.

  • Fire with Property Damage. The fire causes property damage that may or may not make the

premises uninhabitable.

  • Fire without Property Damage. The fire does not cause property damage and may or may not

result in premises being uninhabitable.

6. LAW ENFORCEMENT ACTIVITY. Law enforcement activity that occurs during the provision of service or for which an individual is the subject of a law enforcement investigation that may lead to criminal charges against the individual. This includes law enforcement responding to a possible crime when an individual is in the community or in a vehicle.

  • Individual Charged with a Crime/Under Police Investigation. When an individual is formally

charged with a crime by the police or when an individual is informed, he or she is suspected of committing a crime, and charges may be forthcoming. All charges or suspected charges related to a Behavioral Health Crisis Event should be reported as such and not as law enforcement activity.

  • Licensed Service Location Crime. A crime such as vandalism, break-ins, threats, or actual

occurrences of acts that may result in harm, etc. that occur at a Shared Support service location.

7. MISSING INDIVIDUAL. An individual is considered missing when they are out of contact for more than 24 hours without prior arrangement or the individual is in immediate jeopardy when missing for any period. Based on an individual’s history, safety skills, and familiarity with the area, an individual may be considered in jeopardy before 24 hours elapse. In addition, when police are contacted about a missing individual or the police independently find and return an individual, this is a reportable incident regardless of the amount of time an individual has been missing.

  • In Jeopardy. The unexpected or risky absence of any duration for an individual whose absence

constitutes an immediate danger to the individual or others.

8. NEGLECT. The failure to obtain or provide the needed services and supports defined as necessary or otherwise required by law, regulation, policy or plan (ISP, Behavior Support Plan, safety plan, etc.). This includes acts that are intentional or unintentional regardless of the obvious occurrence of harm.

  • Failure to Provide Medication Management. An event that may cause harm or lead to

inappropriate medication use while the medication is in the control of the person(s) charged with administration. Incidents of this nature include when harm occurs to the individual, the

medication error occurs over more than one consecutive administration or an individual receives medication intended for another individual.

Incidents of this type include but are not limited to a: 1) failure to administer medications via the correct route; 2) failure to implement medication changes in a timely manner; 3) failure to obtain medications from the pharmacy.

  • Failure to Provide Needed Care. The failure to obtain or provide the needed services and

supports. This includes, but is not limited to: 1) failure to implement medical, social, behavioral and restrictive procedures as outlined in the ISP; 2) failure to provide needed care such as food, clothing, personal hygiene, prompt and adequate medical care, emergency services and other basic treatment and necessities needed for development of physical, intellectual, emotional capacity and well-being; 3) failure to obtain, keep in working order or arrange for repair or replacement of equipment such as glasses, dentures, hearing aids, walkers, wheelchairs, etc.; 4) failure to intercede on behalf of the individual with regards to reporting or acting or changes to healthcare needs or failure to ensure medical equipment is repaired or replaced as needed.

  • Failure to Provide Needed Supervision. The failure to provide attention and supervision, including

leaving individuals unattended. This is based upon the supervision care needs in the ISP or recommendations or requirements from a court of law or as a condition of probation/parole.

  • Failure to Provide Protection from Hazards. The failure to protect an individual from health and

safety hazards as part of routine care, service provision or as outlined in the ISP. Examples of failure to provide protection from health and safety hazards include, but are not limited to: 1) failure to prepare and serve food required by an individual’s medical diagnosis; 2) failure to provide protections from poisonous materials; 3) failure to provide shelter and basic utilities; 4) failure to provide basic protections from environmental hazards such as exposure to the sun, extreme elements and other weather-related conditions; 5) failure to regulate water temperatures; 6) failure to provide protection from hazardous activities such as the manufacture, distribution, exposure to and use of illegal drugs.

  • Moving Violation. Any staff or volunteer receiving a moving violation citation during the provision

of services to an individual regardless if operating an entity’s vehicle or personal vehicle.

9. PASSIVE NEGLECT. The inability to provide supports due to environmental factors which are beyond the control of an unpaid caregiver because of lack of experience, information, resources or ability. Passive neglect is reportable if there are no current risk mitigation strategies in the ISP that specifically address the area of passive neglect. .

  • Inability to Provide Medical/Personal Care. The inability of an unpaid caregiver to provide

adequate medical or personal care due to lack of education, training, resources or the physical ability of the caregiver to perform such tasks. This includes the inability to obtain or maintain communication devices, mobility aides and other durable medical equipment.

  • Inability to Provide Necessities. The inability of an unpaid caregiver to provide food, clothing,

adequate housing, utilities or other basic necessities that are essential to maintain the health and safety of an individual.

10. RIGHTS VIOLATION. An unauthorized act which improperly restricts or denies the human or civil rights of an individual, including those rights which are specifically mandated under applicable law, regulation, policy or plan. This includes acts that are intentional or unintentional regardless of the obvious occurrence of harm.

  • Civil/Legal. Any violation of civil or legal rights afforded by law. This includes the right to vote,

speak freely, practice religious choice, access law enforcement and legal services, as well as participate in local, state or national government activities.

  • Communication. The failure to support an individual to communicate at all times. This includes a

failure to obtain needed communication evaluations, assistive devices or service; provide communication support; or maintain communication devices in working order. Communication

includes but is not limited to 1) display of texts in fonts and sizes that meet communication needs; 2) access to sign language interpreters; 3) access to translation to preferred languages; 3) access to persons that can facilitate an individual’s unique communication style; 4) access to braille materials and other tactile communication assistance: 5) access to plain-language materials.

  • Health. The failure to support choice and opportunity related to health care. This includes failure

to inform and educate an individual about physical or behavioral health evaluations and assessments, changes in health status, diagnosis information, test results, medications, treatment options, etc. This also includes the denial of the right of an individual to make informed health care decisions.

  • Privacy. Any violation of an individual’s safely exercised choice to be free from being observed or

disturbed by others. This includes an individual’s choice to maintain the privacy of his or her physical person, living area, possessions, electronic social media (emails, posts on the internet, accounts, content or any similar items), communication with others whether in face to face meetings, phone email, physical mail or any other correspondence, use of image or likeness without the expressed consent of the individual (includes videos or photos taken of the individual for promotional, marketing or any other purposes), or any similar area where a reasonable expectation of privacy exists.

  • Services. Any violation of an individual’s right to control services received. This includes when an

individual refuses to participate in, voices a concern about or wants to make a change to a service, and the ISP team does not address these choices. Individuals have the right to participate in the development and implementation of their ISPs and can choose where, when and how to receive needed services. This also includes the right to control specific schedules and activities related to services.

  • Unauthorized Restrictive Procedure. Any restrictive procedure (other than a physical, chemical or

mechanical restraint) that does not follow ODP’s guidelines related to restrictive procedures or is prohibited by ODP. Restrictive procedures limit an individual’s movement, activity or function; interfere with the individual’s ability to acquire positive reinforcement; result in the loss of objects or activities that an individual values; or require an individual to engage in a behavior in which, given the freedom of choice, the individual would not engage.

11. SELF NEGLECT. An action or lack of action by an individual that results in the individual denying himself or herself proper care, supports and services. Self-neglect is reportable if there are no current risk mitigation strategies in the ISP that specifically address the area of self-neglect.

  • Environmental. Hazardous or unsafe living conditions (i.e., improper wiring, no indoor plumbing,

no heat, no running water, hoarding conditions, unsanitary or unclean living quarters such as animal or insect infestation, no functioning toilet, fecal or urine odors or grossly inadequate housing or homelessness).

  • Medical. The refusal by an individual to take medications on a regular basis; ignoring acute or

chronic health or medical problems; refusal to obtain, use or maintain prescribed medical devices (i.e., eyeglasses, hearing aids, dentures) needed to maintain health and safety.

  • Personal Care/Nutrition. Refusal to consistently wear or obtain appropriate or adequate clothing

for activities or weather conditions, refusal to maintain proper hygiene that presents a serious risk to health or safety or refusal to maintain a proper diet which may lead to malnutrition, illness or dehydration.

  • Other. Other forms of self-neglect may include refusing to accept services or supports that are

essential to maintain health and safety.

12. SERIOUS ILLNESS. A physical illness, disease or period of sickness that requires hospitalization. This includes an elective surgery that requires a hospitalization.

  • Chronic/Recurring. An illness, condition or disease that is persistent or otherwise long-lasting in

its effects for which an individual has had previous treatment or diagnosis.

  • New. An acute illness, condition or disease for which an individual has not previously received

treatment. This includes acute illnesses, conditions or diseases that may become chronic in the future.

13. SERIOUS INJURY. Any injury that requires treatment beyond first aid. This includes injuries that receive an assessment or treatment at an emergency room, urgent care center, primary care physician office, etc. or that require hospitalization. Assessment by emergency medical services that did not require a visit to one of the previously listed locations for treatment is not reportable. Serious injuries that are treated by a medical professional (i.e., doctor, nurse, etc. that is used by the organization) on-site are reportable. Examples include, but are not limited to:

Fractures Dislocations Burns Electric shock Loss or tearing of body parts. Eye emergencies Ingestion of toxic substance. Head injuries from accidents, falls or blows to the head. Any injury with loss of consciousness. Medical equipment malfunction or damage that requires immediate intervention. Lacerations requiring stitches, staples or sutures to close.

o Choking. When food or other items become lodged in the back of the throat and the cause is not attributed to neglect. Choking incidents are only reportable when they require interventions, such as back blows, abdominal thrusts or the Heimlich Maneuver.

  • Injury Accidental. Injury (other than self-inflicted) with a known cause at the time of the report.
  • Injury Self-Inflicted. Injury with a known cause at the time of the report that can be attributed

to an intentional action of an individual to cause harm upon himself or herself.

  • Injury Unexplained. An injury with no known cause at the time of the report.
  • Medical Equipment Failure/Malfunction. Any medical equipment failure or malfunction that

requires intervention by a medical professional. This does not include routine maintenance or care of medical equipment.

  • Pressure Injury (decubiti, pressure ulcer, pressure sore, bedsore). Injuries to skin and underlying

tissue resulting from prolonged pressure on the skin, regardless of stage and including an injury that is unstageable. This includes initial diagnoses, newly affected areas of the body, as well as diagnosis that becomes worse over time.

14. SEXUAL ABUSE. Any attempted or completed nonconsensual sexual act. This act may be physical or non- physical and achieved by force, threats, bribes, manipulation, pressure, tricks, violence or against an individual who is unable to consent or refuse. Sexual abuse includes any act or attempted act that is sexual in nature between a paid service provider staff and an individual regardless of consent on the part of the individual.

Examples of methods used to commit sexual abuse include, but are not limited to:

Use of intimidation or threat of physical force toward an individual in order to gain compliance with a sexual act (i.e., pinning the victim down, assaulting the victim). Administering alcohol or drugs to an individual in order to gain compliance with a sexual act (i.e., drink spiking). Taking advantage of an individual who is unable to provide consent due to intoxication or incapacitation from voluntary consumption of alcohol, recreational drugs or medication. Exploitation of vulnerability (i.e., immigration status, disability, undisclosed sexual orientation, age). Misuse of authority (i.e., using one’s position or power to coerce or force a person to engage in sexual activity).

Economic coercion, such as bartering of sex for basic goods like housing, employment/wages, immigration papers or childcare. Degradation, such as insulting or humiliating an individual. Fraud, such as lies or misrepresentation of a target’s identity. Continual verbal pressure, such as when an individual is being worn down by someone who repeatedly asks for sex or, for example, by someone who complains that the individual does not love them enough. False promises by the target (i.e., promising marriage, promising to stay in the relationship, etc.). Grooming and other tactics to gain an individual’s trust. Control of an individual’s sexual behavior/sexuality through threats, reprisals, threats to transmit sexually transmitted infections (STIs), threats to force pregnancy, etc.

  • Rape. The penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object,

or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of an individual. This includes when an individual was made, or there was an attempt to make the individual, penetrate another person (including the target).

  • Sexual Harassment. Sexual advances that do not involve physical contact between an individual

and a target. This type of sexual abuse can occur in many different venues (i.e., home, school, workplace, in public or through technology). Examples include, but are not limited to:

Sending unwanted sexually explicit photographs. Use of inappropriate sexual remarks or language. Unwanted exposure to sexual situations – pornography, voyeurism, exhibitionist. Threats of sexual abuse to accomplish some other end, such as threatening to rape an individual if he or she does not give the target money. Threatening to spread sexual rumors if the individual does not have sex with the target. Unwanted filming, taking or disseminating photographs of a sexual nature of an individual (in any medium to include, but not limited to, social media, personal computers, cell phones, etc.). Exposure to unwanted sexual materials (pornography).

o Unwanted Sexual Contact. Intentional touching or molesting, either directly or through the clothing, of the genitalia, anus, groin, breast, inner thigh, buttocks or any other body part without consent. This includes making an individual touch or molest another person (including the target).

  • Other. Any sexual abuse of an unknown type at the time of the report or sexual abuse that does

not conform to other secondary category options.

15. SITE CLOSURE. The emergency closure of a licensed or provider operated service location for one (1) or more days. This is reported as a site incident report and does not apply to individuals who reside in homes owned, rented or leased solely by the individual or family member.

  • Infestation. The closure of a site due to the need to treat for animal, insect or other pests.
  • Loss of Utilities. The closure of a site due to loss of utility that was not related to a failure on the

part of the operation entity. This includes electrical outages, issues with water or sewer systems and heating or cooling system failures.

  • Natural Disaster/Weather Related. The closure of a site due to a natural disaster or weather

conditions.

  • Structural. The closure of a site due to structural issues.
  • Other. The closure of a site due to a reason other than infestation, loss of utilities, natural

disaster or weather related or structural issue.

16. SUICIDE ATTEMPT. The intentional and voluntary attempt to take one’s own life. A suicide attempt is limited to the actual occurrence of an act and does include suicidal threats or ideation. If medical treatment was sought after a suicide attempt, it should be reported under suicide attempt as a primary category in all cases, and not as serious injury or illness.

  • Injury/Illness that Requires Medical Intervention. An individual sustained an injury or became ill

due to a suicide attempt and required medical treatment beyond basic first aid.

  • No Injury/Illness that Requires Medical Intervention. An individual did not sustain an injury or

become ill due to a suicide attempt and did not require medical treatment beyond first aid.

B. The following incidents are to be reported within 72 hours:

1. Physical Restraint. A physical hands-on method that restricts, immobilizes or reduces an individual’s ability to move his or her arms, legs, head or other body parts freely. A physical restraint may only be used in the care of an emergency to prevent an individual from immediate physical harm to herself or himself or others. Restraints that are permitted by ODP policies and procedures, regulations or laws are to be reported as physical restraints. All other restraints shall be reported as abuse.

  • Human Rights Team Approved Restrictive Intervention. Any physical restraint that is applied in an

emergency situation that is part of an approved ISP that contains a restrictive procedure.

  • Provider Emergency Protocol. Any physical restraint that is applied in an emergency situation that

is part of the provider emergency restraint protocol. This restraint is not part of an individual approved ISP that contains a restrictive procedure.

2. Medication Error. Any practice that does not comply with the “Rights of Medication Administration” as described in the ODP Medication Administration Training Course. A medication error occurring during a time when an unpaid caregiver is responsible for the administration of medication is reportable. An individual’s refusal to take medication is reportable as a medication error.

  • Wrong Medication. Individual is given a medication that the individual is not prescribed or has

been discontinued, or the individual was given medication that was supposed to be given for another reason.

  • Wrong Dose. Individual is given too much or too little medication during a scheduled

administration.

  • Wrong Time. Individual is given medication too early or too late as defined by the range of

allowable administration time (reportable if medication is given in excess of one hour either prior or later than the prescribed administration time).

  • Wrong Route. Individual is given medication in a different way from the one specified on the

label.

  • Wrong Form. Individual is given medication in a different type from the one prescribed.
  • Wrong Position. Individual is not positioned correctly to receive the medication.
  • Wrong Technique/Method. Medication is prepared for administration improperly.
  • Omission. An administration of medication fails to occur.
  • Wrong Person. An individual is given another individual’s medication.

C. Incidents to be Reported When Directed. ODP will provide specific guidance and direction on what to report, as

well as the timelines to report, related to the following emergencies:

  • Declared Emergency. An event, such as an occurrence of a natural catastrophe, technological

accident or human-caused event that has resulted in, or could potentially cause, severe property damage, deaths and/or multiple injuries such as, but not limited to, public health emergencies, emergency declarations, major declarations, etc. A Declared Emergency is declared by the Federal, State, County or Municipal officials.

  • Public Health Emergency. An event such as a disease or natural disaster that causes, or has the

potential to cause, harm to a significant number of individuals and is declared as a Public Health Emergency by Federal or State officials. Public Health Emergencies are to be reported within timeframes that are specified to the nature of the event and as directed by ODP.

Outbreaks. The occurrence of disease cases in excess of normal expectancy. The number of cases varies according to the disease-causing agent, and the size and type of previous and existing exposure to the agent.

Epidemic. A disease that affects a large number of people within a community, population or region. Pandemic. A disease that affects a large number of people that is spread over multiple countries or continents. Natural Disasters. An event such as a flood, earthquake, storms, hurricanes, tornados, blizzards, etc. Bio-Terrorist Attacks. The intentional release or dissemination of biological agents. These agents are bacteria, viruses, insects, fungi or toxins and may be in a naturally occurring or a human-modified form.

faxed to the appropriate regional ODP office within the designated timeframes. (See attachment A) b. The EIM report will then be entered and submitted as soon as EIM is available. 2. Appropriate county representative(s) will be notified of the incident within the specified time frame, either 24 hours or 72 hours depending upon the category of the incident as defined in this policy. 3. Family members or guardian will be contacted as designated in the individual’s plan. If the person requests that family members not be notified, this will be noted in the EIM report. 4. If investigation is required, point person will notify appropriate agency personnel and a certified investigator will be assigned. 5. The final section of the standardized incident report, those used for incidents reportable within 24 hours, will be completed within 30 days. If the incident report cannot be finalized within 30 days, an extension will be requested via EIM to the county and regional office of ODP prior to the expiration of the 30-day period. 6. A review will occur to ensure the following occurred and will be included in the EIM report: a. Documentation that the health, safety and rights of the individual were protected upon discovery

of the incident. b. Correct incident category was chosen – service location, provider type and service delivery model

are correct. c. The description of the incident is correct and clearly written with details to describe the event. d. An investigation occurred when required - the results of the incident investigation. e. Target(s) identified per the bulletin. f. No identifying information of another individual is included in the report.

g. Corrective actions taken including appropriate safeguards to reduce reoccurrence; discharge and

follow up instructions related to any medical services is included in an incident involving medical care; dates any actions were implemented or planned to be implemented. h. Staff responsible for follow actions is noted. i. All required notifications were made. j. Specific information regarding disciplinary actions taken with staff to assure the health and welfare of individuals. k. An administrative review of the investigation occurred (separate review document is maintained –

Initial Reporter’s responsibilities are as follows (when the initial reporter a staff or volunteer at SSI): a. Respond to the situation by taking immediate action to protect the individual’s health, safety and

rights. b. Report to program leadership or contact on-call agency (point person) to report incident as soon

a. First confirm that appropriate actions have been taken or order additional actions to secure the

expressed. c. If the incident involves abuse, suspected abuse, or alleged abuse, ensure the target is separated

Adult Protective Services Child Protective Services Older Adult Protective Services The individual and person’s designated by the individual, unless the person designated

e. Determine whether an investigation or other follow-up is needed. f. Secure the scene of an incident when an investigation may be required. g.
