II. Adult Protective Services (APS) Reporting Requirements

A. The Adult Protective Services Act (Act 70 of residents of the Commonwealth from abandonment, abuse,

exploitation and neglect. The Act protects people between the ages of 18 and 59 years of age who have a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities. The following categories must be reported immediately if an administrator or employee has reasonable cause to suspect.

1. Abandonment. The desertion of an adult by a caregiver. 2. Abuse. The occurrence of one or more of the following acts: i. The infliction of injury, unreasonable confinement, intimidation or punishment with resulting physical harm, pain or mental anguish. ii. The willful deprivation by a caregiver of goods or services which are necessary to maintain physical or mental health. iii. Sexual harassment, rape or abuse. Does not include environmental factors which are beyond the control of an adult or a caregiver including, but not limited to, inadequate housing, furnishings, income, clothing or medical care. 3. Exploitation. An act or course of conduct by a caregiver or other person against an adult or an adult’s resources, without the informed consent of the adult or with consent obtained through misrepresentation, coercion or threats of force that results in monetary, personal or other benefit, gain or profit for the perpetrator or monetary or personal loss to the adult.

4. Neglect. The failure to provide for oneself or the failure of a caregiver to provide goods, care or services essential to avoid a clear and serious threat to the physical or mental health of an adult. The term does not include environmental factors that are beyond the control of an adult or the caregiver, including, but not limited to, inadequate housing, furnishings, income, clothing or medical care. B. Reporting Format

1. Immediately upon suspicion of abandonment, abuse, exploitation or neglect, make an oral report to the statewide Protective Services Hotline by call 1-800-490-8505. Once the report is made, it will be referred to the APS agency for handling. 2. Within 48 hours of making the oral report, submit a written report to Liberty Healthcare at mandatoryron@libertyhealth.com or fax to 484-434-1590. Submission of the HCSIS or EIM Incident Management report to the Liberty Healthcare email or fax noted above is an acceptable form of written reporting. C. Additional Reporting Requirements as required by the Adult Protective Services Law.

1. An administrator or an employee who has reasonable cause to suspect that the individual is the victim of sexual abuse, serious injury, serious bodily injury or that a death is suspicious, will:

i. Immediately make an oral report to law enforcement officials. An employee should also immediately notify the organization’s administrator unless such notification would jeopardize the investigation or subject the individual to further risk. ii. Immediately make an oral report to the Department of Human Services by calling the mandatory abuse reporting line at 717-265-7887 and selecting option #3. Be prepared to provide your name and telephone number, name of the facility and license number (if applicable or known), the alleged victim’s name, the alleged victim’s date of birth, the type(s) of alleged abuse or neglect, the date and time of the oral report to law enforcement. iii. The administrator and employee will make a joint written report within 48 hours of making the oral report to law enforcement officials. Submission of the HCSIS or EIM Incident Management report is an acceptable form of written reporting. 2. Definitions for Additional Reporting Requirements. i. Serious Bodily Injury. An injury which creates a substantial risk of death or which causes serious permanent disfigurement or protracted loss or impairment of the function of a body member or organ. ii. Serious Injury. An injury that causes a person severe pain or significantly impairs a person’s physical functioning, either temporarily or permanently. iii. Sexual Abuse. Intentionally, knowingly or recklessly causing or attempting to cause rape, involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, sexual assault, statutory sexual assault, aggravated indecent assault or incest.

Rape: a person commits rape when he or she engages in sexual intercourse with

a complainant: (1) by forcible compulsion; (2) by threat of forcible compulsion that would prevent resistance by a person of reasonable resolution; (3) who is unconscious or where the person knows that the complainant is unaware that the sexual intercourse is occurring; (4) where the person has substantially impaired the complainant’s power to appraise or control his or her conduct by administering or employing, without the knowledge of the complainant, drugs, intoxicants or other means for the purpose of preventing resistance; (4) who suffers from a mental disability which renders the complainant incapable of consent; (6) who is less than 13 years of age. Involuntary Deviate Sexual Intercourse: A person commits involuntary deviate

sexual intercourse when he or she engages in deviate sexual intercourse with a complainant: (1) by forcible compulsion (forcible compulsion includes, but is not limited to compulsion resulting in another person’s death, whether the death occurred before, during or after sexual intercourse); (2) by threat of forcible compulsion that would prevent resistance by a person of reasonable resolution; (3) who is unconscious or where the person knows that the complainant is unaware that the sexual intercourse is occurring; (4) where the person has substantially impaired the complainant’s power to appraise or control his or her conduct by administering or employing, without the knowledge of the

complainant, drugs, intoxicants or other means for the purpose of preventing resistance; (5) who suffers from a mental disability which renders him or her incapable of consent; (6) who is less than 13 years of age, or (7) who is less than 16 years of age and the person is four or more years older than the complainant and the complainant and person are not married to each other. Sexual Assault. Except as provided under the definitions relating to rape and

involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, a person commits sexual assault when that person engages in sexual intercourse or deviate sexual intercourse with a complainant without the complainant’s consent. Statutory Sexual Assault. Except as provided under the definition of rape, a

person commits statutory sexual assault when that person engages in sexual intercourse with a complainant under the age of 16 years and that person is four or more years older than the complainant and the complainant and the person are not married to each other. Aggravated Indecent Assault. Except as provided under the definitions relating to

rape, statutory sexual assault, involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, and sexual assault, a person who engages in penetration, however slight, of the genitals or anus of a complainant with a part of the person’s body for any purpose other than good faith medical hygienic or law enforcement procedures commits aggravated indecent assault if: (1) the person does so without the complainant’s consent; (2) the person does so by forcible compulsion; (3) the person does so by threat of forcible compulsion that would prevent resistance by a person of reasonable resolution; (4) the complainant is unconscious or the person knows that the complainant is unaware that the penetration is occurring; (5) the person has substantially impaired the complainant’s power to appraise or control his or her conduct by administering or employing without the knowledge of the complainant, drugs, intoxicants or other means for the purposes of preventing resistance; (6) the complainant suffers from a mental disability which renders him or her incapable of consent; (7) the complainant is less than 13 years of age; or (8) the complainant is less than 16 years of age and the person is four or more years older than the complainant and the complainant and the person are not married to each other. Incest. A person commits incest if he or she knowingly marries or cohabits or has

sexual intercourse with an ancestor or descendant, brother or sister of the whole or half blood or an uncle, aunt, nephew or niece of the whole blood. The relationships referred to include blood relationships without regard to legitimacy, and relationship of parent and child by adoption. Sexual Harassment. Sexual Harassment is unwelcome sexual advances, requests

for sexual favors, and other verbal or physical conduct of a sexual nature.

NOTE:

Sexual Harassment is an abuse that requires reporting to the protective services hotline; however, the APS Act makes a distinction between sexual harassment and sexual abuse – sexual abuse is considered one of the 4 serious and requires additional reporting steps to the Department of Human Services/Adult Protective Services Division and local law enforcement.

IV. Administrative Review Committee/Process

A. Shared Support will have an Administrative Review Committee to conduct the final stage of the investigatory

process (as required by the ODP Announcement – ODP Communication Number 053-18). The committee will thoroughly review each investigation, following the ODP Administrative Review Process guidelines, evaluating the quality of the investigation and determining the final outcome of Confirmed, Not Confirmed or Inconclusive. See Attachment B. The committee will consist of not less than 2 but not more than 5 organizational representatives from administration, risk management, quality assurance, certified investigators not assigned to the case and/or

program representatives. The committee will meet on an ad hoc basis, meeting frequently enough to assure that the investigation can be closed within the 30-day mandated timeframe.

The Certified Investigator will make no reference and give no opinion as to the potential outcome of the investigation within the body of the Certified Investigation Report. The Administrative Review of the report must be completed before finalization of both the investigation, as well as the final incident report

V. Risk Management

A. Shared Support conducts a monthly Risk Management Committee. The Committee has the following

responsibilities.

1. Monitor and document individuals incident data to include the following: a. Evaluation of the effectiveness of incident corrective actions for all incident categories. b. If restraints were utilized, the circumstances surrounding the use of and the frequency of the

restraints for detection of potential abuse. c. Evaluation of data to ensure the least restrictive measures are implemented to support the person,

with the focus on the reduction of restrictive procedures. d. Circumstances and frequency of medication error for detection of potential abuse or neglect. e. Identification and implementation of preventative measures to reduce: 1) the number of incidents;

2) the severity of the risks associated with the incident; 3) the likelihood of an incident reoccurring. f. Documentation of:

o Any need to revise an ISP with the ISP team to include new and/or revised information, risk mitigation strategies or a change in services or supports. o The need to consult with a County ID Program/AE for assistance related to monthly data monitoring, if necessary. o The actions and outcomes of any activities that occurred related to the monthly data monitoring. 2. Review and analyze incident data compiled from the Department’s EIM system quarterly in order to make data-driven decisions regarding supports and service delivery and to identify strategies necessary for improvement. Data review will include the following: a. Review to determine preventable incidents. b. Information on incident targets. c. Identification of root cause of incidents, when possible. d. Develop recommendations to reduce preventable incidents. e. Develop recommendations to reduce the use of restrictive procedures. f. Identify risk factors. g. Develop strategies to mitigate and manage presenting risk factors. h. Identify possible areas of necessary training for support personnel. i. Ensure that support personnel have been training in preventing, recognizing, reporting and responding to incidents. j. Provide recommendations to Program Specialists for additional trainings, risk mitigation strategies and/or recommendations for changes to individual ISPs as well as identified trends or systemic issues. k. Make recommendations to leadership regarding Quality Management initiatives based off of systemic

trends identified through risk analysis.

3. Program Specialists will participate in Risk Management Committee and will ensure Committee’s recommendations are implemented. Will also ensure that the following are included in individuals’ ISPs:

a. Risk factors b. Health status, family medical history and medical risks c. Medication history and current medication

d. Behavioral history and behavior risks e. Incident history f. Social environmental needs g. Physical environmental needs h. Personal safety

4. Program Specialists will also ensure that support personnel and participants are trained on participant risk factors and risk mitigation strategies. 5. Program Specialists will also ensure that risk mitigation strategies are updated as needed and as recommended by the Risk Management Committee.

6. All agency Certified Investigators will participate in a peer review of incident investigations. The reviews will follow the ODP Certified Investigator handbook and training. Investigators will report to Risk Management Committee quarterly.

7. A three-month trend analysis will be conducted and documented for all incident categories. Based on the results of the trend analysis, Shared Support will develop, implement and document both individual specific and agency-wide risk mitigation activities. The analysis must include the following:

  • An analysis of compliance with regulatory timeframes for reporting, investigations and finalization

of incidents.

  • Evaluation of effectiveness of corrective actions for all incident categories.
  • Evaluation of effectiveness of education to the individual, staff and others based on the

circumstances of the incident.

  • A review and trend analysis of comments from the County ID Program/AE and ODP initial

management review and disapproval reasons from the final management review.

  • Any measures that have been implemented or will be implemented to reduce the number of

incidents, the severity of risks associated with the incident and the likelihood of an incident reoccurring.

  • Documentation of the actions and outcomes of any activities that occurred related to the trend

analysis.

VII. Release of Incident Report Information

Upon request by the individual, or persons designated by the individual, Shared Support, Inc. will release incident information including:

1. A summary of the incident report to include a description of the incident, the immediate action(s) taken to protect the health, safety and well-being of the individual, incident classification and all notification information to include date and person or entity notified. 2. The findings, to include additional information and investigation findings and determination (when applicable). *The investigation file is not to be given and any information within the incident information released must have names of other individuals and the reporter redacted. 3. The actions, to include corrective actions planned or implemented and medical intervention information. The information will be redacted to exclude information about another individual and the reporter, unless the reporter is the individual who receives the information.

VICTIM’S ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS Victim’s assistance programs and services are resources available to assist individuals physically, emotionally, financially, medically, and legally when the individual is abused or neglected or a victim of a crime. Individuals may access many resources available through victim’s assistance programs even if they do not intend to file criminal charges or proceed within the criminal justice system.

  • Victims have the right to access victim’s assistance programs and services at any time. Individual Support Plan (ISP) team members should offer victim’s assistance directly to the individual. Direct assistance means that the victim is present when options are discussed and offered. Victimization should not be taken lightly as any type of incident can cause emotional, psychological, physical, financial and behavioral consequences for individuals. Signs of trauma from an incident may or may not be present immediately after an event. Victim’s assistance should be offered more than once to ensure that individuals have the full opportunity to process an event and decide the support(s) they wish to access.
  • In Pennsylvania, there is a strong network of victim’s assistance programs, sometimes called “victim/witness units” that can provide help to victims after abuse, neglect, financial exploitation, domestic violence, sexual assault, simple and aggravated assault, harassment, theft, and homicide. Some programs are based in the criminal/juvenile justice system and aid victims as their cases move through those systems. Oher programs are provided by community-based nonprofits, including domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers, which offer services regardless of whether a victim pursues charges or if the case moves forward for prosecution. All victim’s assistance services are free.
  • Many of the supports available to victims of abuse, neglect or a crime include an advocate. Victim’s assistance programs employ specialized advocates to carry out the functions related to their organization. A victim may work with multiple advocates depending on identified needs.
  • Victims have the right to effective communication through supports such as interpreter services, language line, sign language interpreters, and TTY capabilities.
  • The most common providers of victim’s assistance are local rape crisis centers, domestic violence centers and the Office of Victim’s Services.

I. Community-Based Victim’s Services

Community-based agencies, such as domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers, can provide services regardless of whether the victim decides to press charges or if the crime goes through the criminal justice system. Every county in Pennsylvania is covered by domestic violence and rape crisis programs. Some counties also have a general, nonprofit agency that provides services to all crime victims. Services Offered by Domestic Violence Shelters II. • Confidential Hotlines

  • Available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year
  • Provide counseling, crisis intervention, support, information and referrals III. • Shelter
  • 24-hour emergency shelter
  • Safe homes
  • Transitional housing

IV. • Counseling

  • Empowerment counseling
  • Options counseling (identifies victim choices, assesses risks and benefits)
  • Safety planning (assessment of risk and danger, strategies for enhancing safety, identification of potential resources) • Support groups V. • Advocacy
  • Legal advocacy (legal options, preparation and assistance with Protection From Abuse (PFA) forms and filings)
  • Medical advocacy (based in hospitals, clinics)
  • Children’s advocacy (counseling, therapeutic art, music, and play for children in shelters)
  • Accompaniment (legal services, court proceedings, other service providers) VI. • Economic Support
  • Aid in obtaining cash assistance and employment training
  • Help with securing safe, affordable, permanent housing
  • Job training and identification of employment opportunities

VII.

Services Offered by Rape Crisis Centers

  • Free and confidential crisis counseling, 24 hours a day
  • Prevention education programs for schools, organizations, and other public groups
  • Services for the victim’s family, friends, partner, or spouse
  • Information and referrals to other services in the victim’s area
  • Advocates that are available to accompany victims of sexual violence, rape or incest to medical facilities, the police station, and court
  • Advocates that can intervene or act on behalf of the victim’s wishes or needs and assist in navigating the processes within the medical, police, and court systems

VIII. System-Based Victim Service Agencies (Victim/Witness Programs, Office of Victim’s Services) Each county in Pennsylvania has a program that provides services to victims of crime if the case proceeds through the criminal justice system. These programs are usually located in the county’s District Attorney's Office or the Juvenile Probation Office. Once charges are filed, someone from the county program that provides services to victims of crime will usually be in contact with the victim to initiate services. Information provided to the victim may include the following:

  • The victim’s rights as a crime victim
  • How to register for an offender release notification
  • How to receive notification of the right to provide input regarding any release of the alleged perpetrator
  • The victim’s right to receive compensation
  • How to find an advocate
  • How to obtain counseling or therapy
  • How the legal process works
  • How to register for court notifications
  • How to receive notification of the alleged perpetrator’s escape, recapture, or any custody change
  • How to arrange for court accompaniment
  • Assistance with victim impact statements
  • An explanation of post-sentencing/dispositions
  • How to obtain medical advocacy and accompaniment
  • How to receive notification of execution

Shared Support Fleet Safety Program

I. Background

One of the services provided to Shared Support’s individuals is transportation. Operation of motor vehicles by Shared Support’s employees and contractors carries with it substantial responsibility. The duty of safe operation of vehicles extends to: A. Shared Support’s individuals B. Shared Support’s employees C. Shared Support’s contractors D. The Public At-Large Failure to safely operate any vehicle within the scope of our services may result in substantial property damage or bodily injury. Employees, contractors, individuals and other passengers within the vehicles operated by Shared Support are subject to injuries. The vehicles purchased by Shared Support represent a considerable expense of the operations. It is critical for personnel to ensure that such investments are maintained in the best possible condition and the utmost care be taken in their use. Shared Support’s vehicles are exposed to damage due to a collision or other unsafe acts. In view of the legal and moral responsibility placed upon Shared Support for the safe operation of its vehicles, Shared Support’s Fleet Safety Program is outlined. It is broken down into the following categories:

  • Driver Selection
  • Use and Maintenance
  • Accident Reporting
  • Training
  • Use of Employee Vehicles

II. Driver Selection

Driver error continues to be the number one cause of automobile accidents. One of Shared Support’s objectives, therefore, is the proper selection of employees to drive vehicles within the scope of Shared Support’s operations. Our Insurance carrier also anticipates that we will use good judgment, in accordance with industry-accepted parameters, as to whom we permit to operate vehicles within the scope of Shared Support Activities.

The minimum requirements for individuals authorized to operate Shared Support’s vehicles are as follows: (Rare exceptions to these requirements may only be made by the CEO or COO.) 1. Only designated employees or contractors are permitted to drive Shared Support vehicles. 2. Employees or contractors must be a minimum 18 years of age. 3. Employees must possess a valid driver's license in their present state of residence. For those employees who operate a vehicle subject to commercial licenses, they need to possess a commercial driver's license. 4. Employees must have 3 or more years of driving experience. 5. . Employees must demonstrate the aptitude; and other qualifications as outlined in this policy, including but not limited to, the Motor Vehicle Record (MVR) standards. 6. . Satisfactory completion of a vehicle orientation by the site supervisor which may include clearances

of the vehicle; operating features; and wheel chair safety. In addition, a Defensive Driving Course presented as part of the staff orientation. Both of these trainings need to be satisfactorily completed prior to driving a Shared Support vehicle. During the application process and on an annual basis, MVR inspections on employees will be obtained through the relevant Department of Motor Vehicles. Shared Support reserves the right to obtain any personnel’s MVR on a random or more frequent basis. Such MVR examinations will take into consideration the criteria outlined in this Policy. The criteria apply to the operation of motor vehicles whether or not a Shared Support’s Vehicle.

MOTOR VEHICLE RECORD CRITERIA

Driving Records Subject to Probation

º An employee who damages a Shared Support vehicle (interior or exterior) by improper or careless use while not operating the vehicle. º An employee who operates a cell phone one time within a Shared Support’s vehicle for personal reasons within the past 36 months or an employee who uses a cell phone one time in his/her own vehicle while transporting an individual receiving services from Shared Support, within the past 36 months.

Driving Records Subject to Termination

º A driver who has any one or more of the following over the latest 36 months:

- Driving while under the influence of alcohol or drugs (including prescription or non- prescription drugs—See Section IV), drug offense or open container violation. - Failure of an employee to take proper medication to control seizure disorders which results in a preventable accident—See Section IV - Driving in a reckless manner. - Passing a stopped school bus. - Racing or speed contest violation. - . Vehicle manslaughter/homicide. -

Failure to report an accident within the scope of employment with Shared Support

within 24 hours of the accident - Hit and run – leaving the scene of an accident. - Lending an operator’s license or registration to another person.Driving with a suspended or revoked license. - Driving with a temporary operator’s permit. - Suspended License history –have had 3 or more license suspensions as a result of moving violations. - Eluding a police officer. - Felony committed with a motor vehicle. - Foreign citizens with no historical driving record available to Shared Support. - Abusive or unauthorized use of a Shared Support vehicle - Two or more at-fault accidents. - Three or more moving violations. Texting & cell phone violations are considered moving violations because they increase the likelihood of an accident. Seat belt violations are not moving violations. - Speeding 25 mph, or more, above the speed limit. - Speeding 10 mph, or more, above the speed limit while in a school zone. - Employee personal use of a cell phone while driving a Shared Support’s vehicle on two occasions (recognized by Shared Support – no moving violations issued). - Failure to follow this policy regarding vehicle use.

º A driver who has the following over the latest 12 months:

  • More than 2 moving violations and/or at fault accidents within the past 12 months. * Employees are required to notify the Management immediately upon their having a driver's license suspension or revocation. Failure to do so may result in separation from employment.

* An employee is responsible for payment of any traffic citation or similar fine issued. * Employees are required to make Shared Support, Inc. aware of any citations or accidents within 24 hours of the occurrence and to submit copies of citations to their direct supervisor within 24 hours.

III. Vehicle Maintenance & Use

A close second to operator negligence as a cause of automobile accidents is improper vehicle maintenance. Shared Support is committed to providing for proper maintenance of its vehicles. Such action includes the following:

  • The vehicles will have oil and filter changes in accordance with manufacturers’ recommendations.
  • Vehicles will be sent to its automobile servicing facility for comprehensive maintenance inspections on an annual basis. Such inspections will include an examination of all critical operating systems including, but not limited to: brakes, steering, suspension, tires.
  • On a monthly basis, the designated employees will be responsible for an inspection of the vehicle in accordance with the monthly Vehicle Condition Report of Shared Support. Prior to the use of a vehicle, the driver will walk around the vehicle paying attention to any unknown damage; tire under- pressure or damage; leaking fluids or inoperable lights. The vehicle should not be used in the event of a dangerous condition. Employees who note any abnormality in the vehicle's operating condition should immediately notify the Supervisor so that appropriate action can be taken. Additionally, once per quarter, Maintenance will perform a review of each vehicle.
  • Proper care of Shared Support’s vehicle is the responsibility of all employees who use them. For example, there should be no eating, drinking or smoking by employees in the vehicles.
  • Seat Belts are to be worn by all occupants, at all times in Shared Support Vehicles or vehicles used in the course of Shared Support business. It is the responsibility of the driver to make certain that all passengers are wearing seat belts properly before starting the vehicles. Employees are required to immediately notify Shared Support of a defective seat belt condition and/or problem with the proper fitting of seat belt. In no event, is an employee or passenger to ride in a vehicle without proper restraint.
  • Any unsafe activities in the vehicles are to be reported to Management for any necessary review and treatment. This would include, for example, clients whose behaviors cause undue distraction to the driver and/or unwillingness to wear seat belts.
  • Only employees, individuals in their care and authorized individuals are permitted to ride in Shared Support’s vehicles. No other persons are permitted to ride in a Shared Support vehicle.
  • Vehicles are to be used for Shared Support’s operations only. Employees are not permitted to use Shared Support vehicles for personal reasons. Similarly, outings which are primarily for an employee’s personal use (going to the bank, store, etc.) are not permitted.
  • Personal Use of cell phones is not permitted within the Shared Support’s vehicles. In the event that cell phones are required to be used for Shared Support’s operations, the driver needs to safely pull the vehicle over in order to conduct a conversation.

IV. Other Driving Factors

 We are all responsible for assuring that we are in proper physical and mental condition to operate an

automobile. Shared Support employees who are not in proper condition should not drive an automobile, particularly within the scope of employment. Some of the factors to consider are mentioned below.  Use of prescription medications should be in strict conformance with the doctor’s instructions. It is

imperative that:

 The side effects of medications be completely understood and considered when operating an automobile. In no event is a Shared Support employee to operate an automobile if such medications impair the senses or judgment. Even simple cold medications may cause a considered impairment leading to an accident.  In certain cases, medications will be required to control a health matter such as seizures (epilepsy; grand mal, etc.). In Pennsylvania, you are permitted to drive a vehicle if such seizures have not occurred for a period of at least 6 months; a physician submits a medical report to affirm such fact; and medications are taken in accordance with the doctor’s instructions. Shared Support employees who may be subject to such seizures are required to faithfully follow the doctor’s instructions.  Some people may be subject to blackouts; fainting spells or similar physical problems due to heart-related or circulatory ailments. No employee subject to such condition is permitted to operate a vehicle unless they have first obtained a doctor’s written verification of their ability to safely operate an automobile and that they take medication in accordance with their doctor’s instruction.  A person with diabetes should also strictly follow their doctor’s advice. This will include taking the proper level of insulin and checking their blood sugar prior to long trips. As necessary, some form of sugar should be kept in the vehicle in the event of low blood sugar.  An accident caused by failure to properly medicate will be grounds for separation from employment.

V. Accident Reporting

Prompt action taken in the event of an accident is extremely important to assure that the facts surrounding an accident are properly documented. Such action as described in this section will also minimize the chance of further personal injury or damage.

All agency vehicles have an Accident Reporting Card in the vehicle glove compartment. If using your own vehicle for transport, employees will maintain an Accident Reporting Card in their glovebox In the event of an accident, the following should be done:

  • The police should be immediately contacted. In the event of any injuries, the police should be informed at such time, so that an appropriate medical response can be made.
  • Contact the Supervisor or Supervisor-on-call. This must be done, as soon as practicable, after the police have been contacted but in no event greater than 2 hours unless due to injury suffered by an employee that prevents such a communication. This will provide Shared Support an opportunity to provide assistance and make an accident investigation.
  • When conditions and/or regulations permit, move the vehicle onto the shoulder or side of the roadway to prevent further damage or other hazards. The first priority is to seek medical attention for any person injured.
  • Keep calm. Be courteous. Don't argue. Make no statement concerning the accident to anyone except the police officer who arrives on the scene. Obtain the officer's name and badge number. Do not admit any responsibility for the accident to anyone. Make no settlement regarding the accident. Simply state the facts to the police officer who responds to the scene.
  • Complete the Accident Information form located in the vehicle glove compartment.
  • Obtain the names and addresses of any witnesses.
  • It is important to relate the facts of the accident as best as possible. This will lead to a proper decision as to the responsibility of the accident. Shared Support’s insurance company will use the information as to how they approach their handling of any claims. Thus, there are critical, legal reasons to relate the facts as they occur to the best of one's ability.
  • Subject to this policy, any employee who fails to notify their Supervisor of an accident within 24 hours may be subject to separation from employment.
  • The police will not respond to every accident situation, particularly, for minor accidents. It becomes that much more important to obtain information from the other driver involved in the accident. This will include their name and driver's license number; as well as all insurance information. In the event that the police do not respond, Shared Support’s management will contact the local police station and file the appropriate information.
  • An employee involved in a motor vehicle accident must submit to drug and alcohol testing if any of the following conditions apply: (1) the employee or any other person involved in the accident requires medical treatment beyond first aid administered at the scene; (2) any vehicle involved in the accident requires towing; or (3) there is a reasonable suspicion of drug or alcohol usage. These conditions apply while operating a vehicle owned, leased or rented by Shared Support, Inc. or while conducting Shared Support, Inc. business.
  • In the event a program participant is in the vehicle at the time of even a minor accident, the person must be seen by their primary care physician, urgent care or at the emergency room immediately following the accident. This follow up care must occur, regardless of how the person reports they are feeling. Discharge instructions must be submitted to the Program Specialist following the appointment.

VI. Training

Since operator error is considered the number one cause of automobile accidents, it is in the best interests of all parties to ensure that those who operate vehicles within the scope of employment are properly educated as to safe driving practices. To this end, training of employees will be conducted as follows:

  • Employees who drive will be required to attend driver safety training sessions offered by Shared Support on a minimum annual basis.
  • As previously advised, a defensive driver course will be required of drivers whose records are subject to Probationary status, as well as any other training deemed necessary by Management.
  • All training sessions will require documentation as to the employee's attendance and understanding of the material presented.
  • The training offered within employee orientations will also include a review of Shared Support Fleet Safety Policy Defensive Driving.

VII. Employee-Owned Vehicles

It may be necessary for employees to use their own automobiles to transport individuals or otherwise use their automobiles for agency use. When employees use their own automobiles for personal or business use, their Personal Automobile insurance coverage will respond first in the event of an accident. Thus, for example, if an employee is involved in an automobile accident while transporting an individual, the damage to an employee's automobile will be covered under the employee's personal automobile insurance policy. Also, liability, if any, to another party would be covered under the employee's personal automobile insurance policy. The employee's Personal Automobile insurance policy will always respond first in such an event because:

  • This is in keeping with the legal requirements of automobile insurance policy forms.
  • The employee, as owner of the vehicle, is responsible for the vehicle operation and any resultant accident. This is subject to the financial responsibility law as outlined by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
  • As operator of the vehicle, the employee is in the best position to maintain control of the automobile. As its continuing policy, Shared Support will subsidize employees for the operation of their own automobiles based upon mileage. Such reimbursement anticipates the inclusion of insurance costs.

Employees, who use their personal automobile for agency business will be subject to the following:

1. Only employees who have a valid driver license will be permitted to operate their vehicles within the scope of employment. A copy of an employee's driver license will be provided by Shared Support employees and maintained on file by Shared Support. Upon expiration of a driver’s license, an updated driver’s license shall be copied and maintained. An employee is responsible to immediately notify Management of their driver’s license being revoked or suspended. Failure to provide immediate notification represents grounds for termination. 2. Employees who operate their personal vehicles within the scope of the agency's business will also provide a copy of their automobile insurance card which validates the provision of insurance covering such vehicle as well as current vehicle registration and inspection information. Upon the expiration of such insurance, the employee will provide to Management a copy of the new Automobile Insurance Card. An employee is responsible to immediately notify Management of any non-renewal or cancellation of their personal Automobile Insurance. Failure to provide immediate notification represents grounds for termination 3. Employees are responsible for advising their Automobile insurance company of the use of their automobile. The employee will be responsible for any additional insurance cost of any amending of such a use classification. It is anticipated that employees will comply with state law and insurance company inquiries in providing information on the use of their personal automobile--- such as garage territory and usage. This is urged since there are Insurance Fraud Statutes in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. 4. Employees are required to maintain current automobile inspections and to submit proof of registration to Shared Support, Inc.

VIII. Monitoring and Documentation of Trips in Vehicles

Shared Support uses iCare Manager (iCM) to track and document all trips made in company-owned and personal vehicles for individual transportation and other approved business purposes.

Employees must clock in and out of each trip in iCM and indicate whether they are using a company vehicle or a personal vehicle. The employee's name is automatically recorded.

  • When using a personal vehicle, employees must enter odometer readings between each destination.
  • When using a company vehicle, employees must record the odometer reading at the beginning and end of their workday.

Trip records entered in iCM are reviewed at least every two weeks by the employee’s supervisor and the Shared Support Fiscal Department.

Disaster Preparedness

Shared Support, Inc. maintains a readiness plan in the event of disaster to ensure communication and safety for staff and the people we support.

I. Emergency Placement

  • All individuals have an alternate placement plan in the event that they are unable to remain in the primary residence as a result of disaster. That placement may be with family members, other homes or hotels. Each person’s relocation plan will be maintained in his/her file at the home.
  • Although an alternate placement plan exists for each person, in the event of a natural disaster, it may be necessary to make diverge from alternate placement. For example, in the event of flooding, particular hotels may not be available. Other placements will be sought in such an event and may include Shared Support office space, other resident’s homes, community emergency shelters, etc.

II. Communication

  • Each residential site will have a universal cell phone charging kit in the event that landline service is interrupted.
  • All homes are equipped with on-call schedule and personnel will contact on call during any event or disaster.
  • On call personnel will contact the Program Director and that person will contact CEO, CPO and COO
  • In the event that any part of this chain is broken, any personnel will directly contact CEO or COO in the event of a disaster. These numbers are also located at each home.
  • Whenever a local emergency support system exists, participants will be supported to enroll in these programs which engage during natural disasters. Community Emergency Response Teams is one example and is specific to each county or region.

III. Emergency Kits

  • Each home and office setting have an emergency kit on site that will be replaced every 5 years will include water, nutrient tabs, KN95 Antiviral Masks, a hand crank combination

LED Flashlight/multi-frequency radio/cell phone charger which does not require batteries or electricity, First Aid supplies and protective thermal wraps.

Power/Heat Source Outage Procedure Policy

All staff and Program Specialists will be counseled on procedures to follow during a power or heat source outage including:

1. Direct support staff will contact on call at first notice of outage.

2. Direct support staff will monitor temperature every 2 hours.

3. Should temperatures drop to 65 degrees in the winter months or rise to 85

degrees in the summer months, staff will again contact on-call.

4. On-call will follow regulations and will arrange for hotel accommodations

should temperatures drop below or rise above regulated temperature

guidelines.

Appendix 1 - Winter Storm Precautions

Shared Support, Inc. operates offices, life sharing homes and community living arrangements in venues known for inclement weather during the winter months, including ice, snow and power outages. It is our responsibility to maintain the same level of care to those we support during inclement weather conditions, while safeguarding the safety of both those we support and our staff members.

The following planning is in place to assure that we meet the needs of those we support while assuring the safety of staff:

➢ Supervisors will assist homes in preparing for winter storms by assuring homes have

adequate food supplies, bottled water and medications in the home for at least three days of self-sufficiency;

➢ Homes located in areas known for lengthy power outages, that have long driveways or

are located in remote locations may be evacuated to a hotel before the storm strikes; ➢ Fleet vehicles will remain parked and off roadways – 911 will be called in the event an

emergency transport for medical reasons is needed; ➢ Staff members will work all shifts as scheduled, preparing ahead of the storm by making

alternate travel arrangements and giving plenty of time for travel to their work site. If a staff member is still having difficulty reporting to work, their direct supervisor or on-call personnel is to be contacted immediately and assistance will be offered when possible; ➢ Staff members on shift during a winter storm are urged to prepare ahead and to remain

flexible in the event their relief co-worker is having difficulty reporting to shift. Staff will be compensated for any additional time spent on shift covering during a winter storm, as well as be compensated for early starts if they plan ahead and make arrangements to arrive to the site before the worst of the storm strikes; ➢ Staff members running late for shift during winter storms are urged to be careful on the

roads and to take their time getting to work – staff will not be penalized for late arrivals during winter snow conditions.

Appendix 2 – Active Shooter Event

An “active shooter” is an individual who is engaged in killing or attempting to kill people in a confined and populated area; in most cases, active shooters use firearm(s) and there is no pattern or method to their selection of victims.

Active shooter situations are unpredictable and evolve quickly. Typically, the immediate deployment of law enforcement is required to stop the shooting and mitigate harm to victims.

Because active shooter situations are often over within 10 to 15 minutes, before law enforcement arrives on the scene, individuals must be prepared both mentally and physically to deal with an active shooter situation.

Appendix 3 – Tornado

Tornadoes are nature’s most violent storms. Spawned from powerful thunderstorms, tornadoes can cause fatalities and devastate a neighborhood in seconds. A tornado appears as a rotating, funnel-shaped cloud that extends from a thunderstorm to the ground with whirling winds that can reach 300 miles per hour. Damage paths can be in excess of one mile wide and 50 miles long. Every state is at some risk from this hazard.

ACTIVE SHOOTER EVENTS

When an Active Shooter is in your vicinity, you must be prepared both mentally and physically to deal with the situation.

You have three options:

Have an escape route and plan in mind

Leave your belongings behind

Evacuate regardless of whether others agree to follow

Help others escape, if possible

Do not attempt to move the wounded

Prevent others from entering an area where the active shooter may be

Keep your hands visible

Call 911 when you are safe

HIDE

Hide in an area out of the shooter’s view

Lock door or block entry to your hiding place

Silence your cell phone (including vibrate mode) and remain quiet

Fight as a last resort and only when your life is in imminent danger

Attempt to incapacitate the shooter

Act with as much physical aggression as possible

Improvise weapons or throw items at the active shooter

Commit to your actions . . . your life depends on it

The first officers to arrive on scene will not

stop to help the injured. Expect rescue

teams to follow initial officers. These rescue

teams will treat and remove injured.

Once you have reached a safe location, you

will likely be held in that area by law

enforcement until the situation is under

control, and all witnesses have been

identified and questioned. Do not leave the

area until law enforcement authorities have

instructed you to do so.

FIGHT

RUN

Some tornadoes are clearly visible, while rain or nearby low-hanging clouds obscure others. Occasionally, tornadoes develop so rapidly that little, if any, advance warning is possible.

Before a tornado hits, the wind may die down and the air may become very still. A cloud of debris can mark the location of a tornado even if a funnel is not visible. Tornadoes generally occur near the trailing edge of a thunderstorm. It is not uncommon to see clear, sunlit skies behind a tornado.

The following are facts about tornadoes:

  • They may strike quickly, with little or no warning;
  • They may appear nearly transparent until dust and debris are picked up or a cloud forms in the funnel;
  • The average tornado moves southwest to northeast, but tornadoes have been known to move in any direction;
  • The average forward speed of a tornado is 30 MPH, but may vary from stationary to 70 MPH;
  • Tornadoes can accompany tropical storms and hurricanes as they move onto land;
  • Waterspouts are tornadoes that form over water;
  • Tornadoes are most frequently reported east of the Rocky Mountains during spring and summer months;
  • Peak tornado season in the southern states is March through May; in the norther states it is late spring through early summer;
  • Tornadoes are most likely to occur between 3:00 p.m. and 9:00 p.m. but can occur at any time.

Know the Terms

Familiarize yourself with the following terms to help identify a tornado hazard:

  • Tornado Watch – This means that tornados are possible. Remain alert for approaching storms. Watch the sky and stay tuned to NOAA Weather Radio, commercial radio or television for information.
  • NOAA is a nationwide network of radio stations broadcasting continuous

weather information from the nearest National Weather Service office. (http://nws.noaa.gov/nwr/)

  • Tornado Warning – This means a tornado has been sighted or indicated by weather radar. Take shelter immediately.

Take Protective Measures

Before a tornado, be alert to changing weather conditions:

  • Listen to NAOO Weather Radio or to commercial radio or television newscasts for the latest information;
  • Look for approaching storms;
  • Look for the following danger signs:
  • Dark, often greenish sky
  • Large hail
  • A large, dark, low-lying cloud (particularly if rotating)
  • Loud roar, similar to a freight train If you see approaching storms or any of the danger signs, be prepared to take shelter immediately.

During a tornado – if you are under a tornado WARNING, seek shelter

immediately.

IF YOU ARE IN:

THEN:

A structure (home, school, restaurant, etc.) Go to a pre-designated shelter area such as a safe room, basement, storm cellar or the lowest building level. If there is no basement, go to the center of an interior room on the lowest level (closet/interior hallway), away from corners, windows, doors and outside walls. Put as many walls as possible between you and the outside. Get under a sturdy table and use your arms to protect your head and neck. Do not open windows. A vehicle, trailer or mobile home Get out immediately and go to the lowest floor of a sturdy, nearby building or a storm shelter. Mobile homes, even if tied down, offer little protection from tornadoes. The outside with no shelter Lie flat in a nearby ditch or depression and cover your head with your hands. Be aware of the potential for flooding. Do not get under an overpass or bridge. You are safer in a low, flat area. Never try to outrun a tornado in urban or congested areas in a car or truck. Instead, leave the vehicle immediately for safe shelter. Watch for flying debris. Flying debris from tornadoes causes fatalities and injuries.

SOURCE: WWW.FEMA.GOV

Preparing a Safe Room

Extreme windstorms in many parts of the country pose a serious threat to buildings and their occupants. An office or residence may be built “to code,” but that does not mean it can withstand winds from extreme events such as tornadoes and major hurricanes. The purpose of a safe room or a wind shelter is to provide a safe space where people can seek refuge that provides a high level of protection. A safe room can be identified in one of several places in your home or office:

  • A basement
  • Atop a concrete slab-on-grade foundation or garage floor
  • An interior room on the first floor

Safe rooms below ground level provide the greatest protection, but a safe room in a first floor, interior room can also provide the necessary protection. Below ground safe rooms must be designed to avoid accumulating water during the heavy rains that often accompany severe windstorms. To protect its occupants, a safe room must be able to withstand high winds and flying debris, even if the rest of the facility is severely damaged or destroyed. Consider the following when identifying a safe room:

  • The safe room must be adequately anchored to resist overturning and uplift;
  • The walls, ceiling and door of the shelter must withstand wind pressure and resist penetration by windborne objects and falling debris;
  • The connections between all parts of the safe room must be strong enough to withstand wind. Additional information about safe rooms is available at: https://www.fema.gov/safe-rooms

Appendix 4 – Hazardous Materials Incident

Hazardous materials come in the form of explosives, flammable and combustible substances, poisons and radioactive materials. Hazards can occur during production, storage, transportation, use or disposal. You are at risk if a chemical is used unsafely or released in harmful amounts into the environment where you live or work, such as a chemical spill on a local highway.

During a Hazardous Material Incident

If you are asked to evacuate:

  • Do so immediately;
  • Stay tuned to a radio or television for information on evacuation routes, temporary shelters and procedures;
  • If you have time, minimize contamination in the home or office by closing all windows, shutting all vents and turning off attic fans;
  • Take disaster supplies, such as personal medications.

If you are caught outside:

  • Stay upstream, uphill and upwind. In general, try to go at least one-half mile from the danger area;
  • Do not walk into or touch spilled liquids, airborne mists or condensed solid chemical deposits. Try not to inhale gases, fumes and smoke. If possible, cover your mouth with a cloth or mask while leaving the area;
  • Stay away from accident victims until the hazardous material has been identified.

If you are in a motor vehicle:

  • Stop and seek shelter in a permanent building;
  • If you must remain in your car, keep the car windows and vents closed and shut off the air conditioner and heater.

If you are directed to remain indoors:

  • Warn everyone outside to enter the building immediately;
  • Bring pets inside;
  • Close and lock all exterior doors and windows. Close vents, fireplace dampers and as many interior doors as possible;
  • Turn off air conditioners and ventilation systems or set ventilations systems to 100 percent recirculation so that no outside air is drawn into the building;
  • If gas or vapors have entered the building, take shallow breaths through a cloth or a towel;
  • Avoid eating or drinking any food or water that may be contaminated;
  • Go into your pre-selected shelter room
  • Move away from windows and move to the core of the building
  • Move everyone to the second floor or higher if in a multistory building
  • Do not occupy the basement

After a Hazardous Materials Incident

Listen to the local radio or television stations for the latest emergency information – once advised that the incident has been contained:

  • Go to a designated public shelter if you have been told to evacuate or you feel it is unsafe to remain in the home or office. Text SHELTER + ZIP Code to 43362 (4FEMA) to find the nearest shelter in your area (example: shelter 12345);
  • Act quickly if you have come into contact with or have been exposed to hazardous chemicals;
  • Follow decontamination instructions from local authorities;
  • Seek medical treatment for unusual symptoms as soon as possible;
  • Place exposed clothing and shoes in tightly sealed containers;
  • Advise everyone who comes in to contact with you that you may have been exposed to a toxic substance;
  • Return home only when authorities say it is safe. Open windows and vents and turn on fans to provide ventilation;
  • Find out from local authorities how to clean land and property;
  • Report any lingering vapors or other hazards to your local emergency services office.

Appendix 5 – Influenza/Pandemic

Introduction:

Seasonal influenza epidemics are caused by influenza viruses, which circulate around the world.

The purpose of this pandemic response plan is to ensure that the health and safety of our staff and individuals is protected while maintaining essential operations and minimizing disruptions to our services. This plan outlines actions to prevent, prepare for, respond to and recover from a pandemic, in alignment with public health guidance.

This pandemic protocol applies to all employees, individuals and homes associated with Shared Support, Inc. The plan will be enacted when a pandemic is declared by the World Health Organization (WHO) or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), or when public health authorities issue relevant guidance.

Guiding Principles:

1. Health and Safety Priority: Safeguarding the health of all individuals associated with Shared Support, Inc. is our top priority. Actions will be taken to prevent the spread of infectious diseases through robust hygiene practices, social distancing, remote work arrangements and rapid response to potential cases. 2. Clear Communication: We will provide transparent, timely and accurate information to individuals, their families, employees, lifesharers, partners and stakeholders. Updates

will be issued regularly and as situations change, including shifts in operational status and new public health guidance. 3. Operational Continuity: We are committed to maintaining critical functions and services with minimal disruption. This may include adjusting staffing, altering service delivery and activating continuity strategies such as remote work or alternate work locations. 4. Responsiveness to Public Health Guidance: Shared Support, Inc. will adhere to directives from federal, state, and local health authorities. Preventative measures and response actions will be adjusted as the pandemic evolves, ensuring our approach remains aligned with the latest public health recommendations. 5. Support for Employees and Stakeholders: Shared Support, Inc. is dedicated to supporting the mental and physical well-being of employees during a pandemic. Resources, such as wellness support and information on community services, will be made available.

Pandemic Response Strategies:

1. Prevention and Preparedness

  • Enact and promote hygiene protocols.
  • Ensure homes and offices are equipped with necessary sanitation supplies and

PPE. Additional supplies are maintained at the Sunbury Office for distribution.

  • Develop flexible work arrangements, such as remote work or staggered shifts. As

our homes are staffed 24/7, these shifts must continue. 2. Monitoring and Detection

  • Implement screening protocols for staff and visitors as needed.
  • Monitor public health reports and communicate updates to all personnel.
  • Conduct regular checks of supplies and resources to ensure availability. 3. Response Actions
  • Increase cleaning, sanitation and air circulation of high-contact areas. Ensure air

purifiers are functional and filters have been replaced per the maintenance schedule.

  • Enact social distancing measures in workplaces. While this is not possible in the

homes, it can be achieved in the office setting and while in the community.

  • Suspend non-essential travel and encourage remote work where possible. 4. Recovery and Resumption
  • Gradually resume normal operations in phases, as public health conditions allow.
  • Debrief and update the pandemic response plan based on lessons learned.
  • Offer continued support to employees re-adjusting to post-pandemic work

environments.

Sources: World Health Organization (WHO) – www.who.int Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) – www.cdc.gov
